strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored gap: most existing user simulators for tool agents are purely cooperative, and this paper systematically introduces four well-motivated categories of non-collaborative behavior grounded in marketing/dialogue literature and real conversational data (LMSYS, WildChat).

The proposed simulator architecture is thoughtfully engineered, combining a collaborative backbone (dialogue state tracker + ending verifier) with additional modules for each non-collaborative behavior, explicitly aiming to preserve goal alignment while injecting realistic friction—an important design goal that is empirically validated via the Goal Alignment / Initial Goal Alignment metrics.

Experiments are extensive: five agent LLMs (open- and closed-source) across two distinct benchmarks (MultiWOZ, adapted into a new agent environment, and τ-bench), with detailed error-type breakdowns (helper API duplication, hallucination, apology rates, parameter hallucination) that provide genuine mechanistic insight into why agents fail under each behavior type rather than just reporting aggregate success-rate drops.

The paper goes beyond single-behavior evaluation to study combined behaviors, fine-tuning transfer (showing SFT on collaborative data alone does not generalize to non-collaborative robustness), and compares against a reasonable prompt-only baseline (PBUS), showing their simulator induces more substantial and controlled performance degradation.

Includes human evaluation for realism and thorough documentation (extensive appendix with prompts, dataset construction, and implementation details), aiding reproducibility and future extension to other benchmarks.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is somewhat limited: the core approach primarily orchestrates existing techniques (LLM-based dialogue state tracking from Laban et al., ending verification inspired by Luo et al., persona-based generation, style transfer) into a pipeline rather than proposing fundamentally new modeling or learning techniques; the contribution is largely a systems/benchmark contribution rather than an algorithmic one.

The human evaluation is fairly limited in scale (30 sampled scenarios, 3 annotators, 180 dialogue judgments) and yields mixed results—e.g., the proposed simulator underperforms PBUS in the tangential mode and only achieves ~60% win rate for combined behaviors—somewhat undercutting the claim that the simulator is clearly more realistic than a simple prompting baseline.

Heavy reliance on LLM judges (GPT-4o-mini/GPT-4.1-mini) for goal alignment verification, tangential response checking, dialogue act classification, etc., raises concerns about compounding evaluation bias/noise, and there is no human validation of these automatic verifiers' accuracy.

The custom MultiWOZ agent environment (helper APIs, book/retrieve API design, 89 selected "book" scenarios) is newly constructed by the authors rather than a standard, widely-adopted benchmark, which raises reproducibility and comparability concerns with future work; details of exact API design choices could meaningfully affect measured degradation.

Some interesting explanatory narratives (e.g., apology-rate correlation with degradation under impatience, Qwen3-235b's hallucination-driven failure vs Qwen3-30b's robustness) are somewhat speculative/post-hoc and based on correlational analysis rather than causal intervention, limiting the strength of the mechanistic claims.

The paper does not explore mitigation strategies in depth (e.g., training agents specifically on non-collaborative data to test whether robustness improves), leaving the practical actionability of the diagnostic framework only partially demonstrated (only one SFT-on-collaborative-only experiment is shown, not the converse).

strengths: Identifies and addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: existing tool-agent user simulators are agent-friendly/cooperative, while real users exhibit unavailable-service requests, tangential chatter, impatience, and incomplete utterances.

The simulator architecture is reasonably well engineered, combining a collaborative backbone (dialogue state tracker + ending verifier) with modular interventions for each non-collaborative behavior, and grounds the behavior taxonomy in prior marketing/dialogue-act literature (Bitner et al., Reynolds & Harris, MIDAS acts).

Broad experimental coverage: two benchmarks (MultiWOZ, tau-bench), five agent LLMs of varying scale/architecture, fine-tuning experiments on smaller models, and a human evaluation comparing against a prompt-only baseline (PBUS).

Provides detailed, model-specific failure-mode analyses (helper-API duplication, API hallucination, apology-loop behavior, parameter hallucination) that offer some actionable insight into why agents degrade under each behavior type.

Goal-alignment (IGA) metric and iterative regeneration procedure is a sensible attempt to disentangle "simulator fails to convey the goal" from "agent genuinely fails under non-collaborative pressure".
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental rather than conceptual: the four behavior categories largely repackage known phenomena (underspecification/missing-parameter dialogues from Laban et al. and Shim et al., open-domain dialogue acts from MIDAS, dysfunctional-customer marketing taxonomies) into an engineering pipeline of LLM calls, rather than offering a new theoretical or modeling contribution.

The main simulator-quality comparison (Ours vs. PBUS) uses a deliberately weak baseline (bare prompting with no additional modules); it is unsurprising that a multi-module pipeline with explicit dialogue-state tracking, persona injection, and style transfer outperforms naive prompting, which limits how much the comparison tells us about the true difficulty/realism gains versus just added engineering complexity.

Human evaluation is small-scale (9 annotators, 180 dialogues sampled from only 30 scenarios) and shows mixed/underwhelming results—e.g., the proposed simulator underperforms PBUS in the tangential condition and only achieves ~60% win rate on combined behaviors—undermining the claim that behaviors are reliably "natural" and realistic.

Many design decisions (anger-escalation probability increments, truncation points for incomplete utterances, number of augmented unavailable-service goals, 30-step reasoning cutoff) appear heuristically chosen without ablations or sensitivity analyses justifying them.

The MultiWOZ agent environment (APIs, DB-write tasks, helper-API scaffold) is custom-built by the authors rather than a standard, independently validated benchmark, which raises reproducibility and comparability concerns with prior/future work, and the 89-scenario subset is quite small.

Analysis sections rely heavily on post-hoc, somewhat speculative explanations ("we hypothesize", "this suggests") for cross-model divergences (e.g., Qwen3-30b vs 235b, GPT-nano complaint sensitivity) without controlled experiments isolating the proposed causal mechanisms.

No statistical significance testing is reported for the many pairwise SR comparisons across models/conditions, despite relatively small sample sizes (89 and 157 scenarios) and some non-monotonic trends (e.g., relative SR >100% for GPT-4.1-nano under impatience) that are not discussed as noise vs. signal.

Fine-tuning experiments are limited to a single epoch, a small set of small models, and training data derived only from collaborative dialogues in one benchmark (MultiWOZ), making the generalizability of the "fine-tuning doesn't transfer to robustness" conclusion uncertain.

The dependence on proprietary LLMs (GPT-4.1-mini, GPT-4o-mini) as the backbone for nearly every simulator module makes the pipeline costly, less reproducible, and potentially confounded by the simulator model's own biases/capabilities, which is not discussed as a limitation.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: nearly all prior tool-agent user simulators are cooperative, limiting realistic training/evaluation.
Well-grounded taxonomy of four non-collaborative behaviors (unavailable service, tangential, impatience, incomplete utterance), each motivated by relevant marketing/dialogue literature.

Thoughtful simulator architecture that layers non-collaborative behavior modules on top of a goal-tracking collaborative backbone (dialogue state tracker + ending verifier) to preserve goal alignment while injecting realistic friction.

Comprehensive experiments spanning two different benchmarks (MultiWOZ, τ-bench), five agent LLMs (closed- and open-source), and detailed per-behavior failure analysis (helper API duplication, hallucinated API results, apology loops, parameter hallucination).
Additional fine-tuning study showing that models trained only on collaborative data generalize poorly to non-collaborative conditions, which is a useful and actionable finding for practitioners.

Includes both automatic (Goal Alignment / Initial Goal Alignment) and human evaluation against a reasonable prompt-only baseline (PBUS), adding some credibility to the claim that induced difficulty reflects genuine behavior realism rather than simulator artifacts.
Extensive appendix with prompts, dataset/API details, and error taxonomies supports reproducibility and extensibility to new benchmarks.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on LLM-based judges (dialogue state tracker, ending verifier, goal-alignment checker, tangential-response checker) that are implemented with the same or similar model families used elsewhere in the pipeline raises concerns about circularity and potential bias in both simulation and evaluation.

Human evaluation is based on a fairly small sample (30 scenarios, 180 dialogue pairs) and yields mixed results (e.g., simulator underperforms PBUS in the tangential dimension), which complicates the claim that the proposed simulator is more realistic overall; no statistical significance testing is reported for SR or human-eval differences.

Some results are counterintuitive and left under-explained (e.g., GPT-4.1-nano's relative SR increasing to 113% under impatience in MultiWOZ), weakening confidence in the consistency of the observed degradation patterns.

The core claim that performance drops reflect 'genuine' agent weaknesses rather than simulator-induced artificial difficulty rests substantially on the IGA metric, which is itself computed by an LLM judge rather than independently validated ground truth.

Comparisons are limited to a single baseline simulator (PBUS, essentially a prompt-only variant of Yao et al. 2024); no comparison to other recent user-simulator approaches (e.g., DuetSim, GRPO-trained simulators cited in related work) is provided.

The success metric (exact DB-state match) may penalize agents for reasonable behavior under non-collaborative conditions (e.g., appropriately declining an unavailable service could still count as task 'failure'), potentially conflating robustness with strict goal completion.

Novelty is somewhat incremental: the four behavior categories and underlying techniques (goal sharding, dialogue-act driven generation, persona-based augmentation) are recombinations of existing ideas rather than fundamentally new mechanisms.
The fine-tuning robustness study is restricted to MultiWOZ only, with a small set of small-scale base models, limiting generality of the conclusions about fine-tuning vulnerability.
No discussion of computational/latency overhead introduced by the many chained LLM modules, which could matter for practical adoption of the framework.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: existing user simulators for tool agents are overwhelmingly cooperative, limiting realistic robustness evaluation; the paper's four-category taxonomy (unavailable service, tangential, impatience, incomplete utterance) is grounded in marketing and user-LLM conversation literature, giving the framework a principled basis.

Extensive and carefully designed experiments across two distinct benchmarks (MultiWOZ, τ-bench) and five diverse agent LLMs (closed- and open-source), revealing consistent and interpretable performance degradation patterns along with behavior-specific failure mechanisms (duplicated helper API calls, API hallucination, excessive apologizing, incomplete task completion due to complaints).

Strong methodological rigor: goal-alignment metric validated against human judgments (MCC=0.77), extensive appendix analyses addressing potential confounds (reasoning step sufficiency, exclusion of retrieval/human-transfer tasks, single- vs multi-domain merges), and human evaluation comparing the proposed simulator against a prompt-only baseline (PBUS) showing higher realism (~60% win rate).

Demonstrates practical utility: fine-tuning experiments show that agents trained only on collaborative data generalize poorly to non-collaborative behaviors, and that mixing non-collaborative training data improves robustness, which has actionable implications for practitioners.
Good extensibility demonstration to additional domains (ColBench, MINT/HotpotQA/HumanEval/TheoremQA/GSM8K), supporting the claim that the framework generalizes beyond booking-style dialogues.
Detailed and transparent reporting of prompts, error taxonomies, and dataset construction, aiding reproducibility despite code/data not yet released.
weaknesses: The taxonomy of four behavior categories, while grounded, is a subjective clustering choice by the authors; coverage completeness and mutual exclusivity of these categories versus other plausible non-collaborative behaviors (e.g., contradictory demands, deception) is not rigorously justified.

Heavy reliance on LLM-based modules (dialogue state tracker, ending verifier, goal-alignment checker, respond checker) built primarily with GPT-4.1-mini/GPT-4o-mini raises concerns about compounding biases and potential self-preference effects, since the same family of models is used both to generate user behavior and to judge/evaluate it (e.g., GA metric, complaint triggers).

Human evaluation, while informative, is relatively small in scale (9 annotators, 30 sampled scenarios per condition), and some behavior combinations show weaker realism scores (e.g., tangential-related combos), which somewhat undercuts the claim of uniformly higher naturalness over PBUS.

In Table 2, PBUS sometimes achieves comparable or higher success rates than the proposed simulator alongside similar IGA scores, complicating the interpretation that the SR gap is solely due to genuinely harder/realistic non-collaborative behavior rather than idiosyncrasies of the more complex pipeline.

The pipeline's substantial complexity (many chained LLM calls per turn for tracking, generation, verification) implies non-trivial computational and API cost, which is not discussed, potentially limiting ease of adoption despite claims of easy extensibility.

The contribution is primarily an evaluation/diagnostic framework rather than a new modeling technique to address the revealed weaknesses; while valuable, this narrows technical novelty relative to venues emphasizing algorithmic contributions.
Code and datasets are promised for release only upon publication, limiting immediate reproducibility verification.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: nearly all prior user simulators for tool agents are purely cooperative, so studying non-collaborative behaviors is a timely and practically relevant contribution.

The four-category taxonomy (unavailable service, tangential, impatience, incomplete utterance) is grounded in marketing and dialogue literature with an explicit selection/clustering rationale in the appendix, giving the design some theoretical backing rather than being purely ad hoc.

Extensive empirical evaluation across two benchmarks (MultiWOZ, tau-bench), five agent LLMs, and combined-behavior settings, with detailed failure-mode analyses (helper API duplication, API result/parameter hallucination, apology rate increases, user complaint counts) that give mechanistic insight into why performance degrades.

Goal-alignment metric is validated against human judgments (MCC 0.77), and a human pairwise evaluation against a prompt-only baseline (PBUS) is conducted, adding some credibility to claims of realism and difficulty.

Extensive appendix work: ablations on reasoning-step limits, single- vs multi-domain MultiWOZ splits, exclusion of human-transfer scenarios with justification, fine-tuning experiments showing collaborative-only training leaves agents vulnerable to non-collaborative behavior, and extensibility demonstrations on ColBench and MINT.
Practical takeaway (mixing non-collaborative data during fine-tuning improves robustness) has direct utility for practitioners deploying tool agents.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is largely an engineering pipeline of heuristic triggers and LLM-based sub-modules (probabilistic anger escalation, rule-based unavailable-goal augmentation, style-transfer for incomplete utterances) rather than a conceptually novel modeling approach; novelty is incremental relative to existing collaborative simulators (Yao et al. 2024, Laban et al. 2025) that the paper builds directly on.

Nearly every stage of the pipeline (dialogue state tracking, ending verification, tangential-response checking, dialogue-act classification, goal-alignment checking) relies on LLM judges, but reliability is validated in only one place (goal alignment, on 40 samples); errors could compound across these many judge calls without being surfaced.

Human evaluation is based on a small sample (30 scenarios, 3 annotators per set) and the explanation for tangential behavior's weaker performance in combined settings (post-hoc claim that certain behavior pairings are 'unnatural') is somewhat circular and could rationalize away unfavorable results rather than being independently validated.

Only a single user-simulator backbone (GPT-4.1-mini/GPT-4o-mini) is used to generate non-collaborative behaviors; there is no analysis of how sensitive the findings are to the choice of simulator LLM, which limits generality of the reported degradation magnitudes.

MultiWOZ is a relatively dated, template-driven benchmark, and the newly constructed MultiWOZ agent environment (with hand-built helper APIs) is not independently validated against any existing agentic execution framework, raising reproducibility/generalizability concerns beyond the two benchmarks studied.

Some findings are somewhat expected/low-insight (e.g., models apologize more under impatience, incomplete utterances cause more hallucinated parameters without full API context), reducing the paper's scientific novelty despite the thoroughness of the analysis.

Fine-tuning experiments demonstrating the practical value of non-collaborative training data are conducted only on MultiWOZ with small 3B/7B models, leaving open whether the conclusions transfer to tau-bench or to larger-scale production settings.

strengths: Addresses a clear and practically important gap: existing user simulators for tool agents are overwhelmingly cooperative, which likely leads to overestimated agent robustness; the paper's four-category taxonomy (unavailable service, tangential, impatience, incomplete utterance) is carefully grounded in marketing and human-LLM conversation literature rather than being ad hoc.

Technically thoughtful simulator design: the collaborative backbone with dialogue state tracker and ending verifier ensures goal alignment even while injecting non-collaborative behaviors, and this is empirically validated via the Initial Goal Alignment metric and human-correlated judge (MCC=0.77).

Extensive and rigorous experimentation: five agent LLMs across two benchmarks, detailed per-behavior error analysis (duplicated API calls, hallucinated API results, apology rates, input-parameter hallucination) that provides mechanistic explanations rather than just aggregate numbers.

Strong comparison against a reasonable baseline (prompt-based user simulator) with both automatic (SR/IGA) and human pairwise evaluation, showing the proposed simulator is both more challenging and rated as more realistic.

Demonstrates practical relevance through fine-tuning experiments showing that models trained only on collaborative data underperform on non-collaborative behaviors, and that mixing non-collaborative training data helps — directly useful for practitioners.
Good extensibility validation on additional domains (ColBench, MINT) beyond the two main benchmarks, supporting the claimed generality of the framework.

Very thorough appendix (prompts, error tables, ablations on reasoning-step limits, excluded test cases, co-occurrence analysis) that substantially aids reproducibility and pre-empts several natural reviewer questions (e.g., step-limit sensitivity, human-transfer confound).
weaknesses: The overall pipeline is a fairly complex composition of several LLM-based modules (goal generator, dialogue state tracker, ending verifier, complaint/impatience generators, style transfer) tuned specifically for MultiWOZ/τ-bench; while extensibility is shown, the amount of manual adaptation logic needed per domain (as described in Appendix F.1) suggests the framework may require nontrivial engineering effort to port to genuinely new domains despite being advertised as 'easily extensible'.

Evaluation scale is modest: 89 MultiWOZ and 157 τ-bench scenarios, and human evaluation is based on only 30 sampled scenarios with 3 (or 9, per inconsistent reporting) annotators, which may limit the statistical robustness of the human-realism claims.

Some explanations for behavior-combination results (e.g., why tangential+impatience or tangential+incomplete-utterance combinations score lower) are somewhat post-hoc narrative justifications rather than being independently validated.

The user simulator itself is built on GPT-4.1-mini/4o-mini, which could bias the 'naturalness' of generated non-collaborative utterances toward this model family's stylistic tendencies, and it is unclear how sensitive results are to the choice of simulator backbone.

Mitigation strategies are only lightly explored (basic SFT with mixed data); the paper does not propose or evaluate more sophisticated training/inference-time defenses, leaving the 'so what should agent developers do' question only partially answered.

The four-category taxonomy, while grounded, still reflects a subjective clustering choice from a much larger space of documented dysfunctional customer/user behaviors, and the paper does not deeply justify why exactly these four (versus, e.g., separating illegitimate complaints from unavailable-service requests) are optimal or exhaustive.
